content: Studies conducted by the CDC have detected bisphenol A (BPA) in the urine of 95% of adults sampled between 1988 and 1994, and in 93% of children and adults tested in 2003–2004. While the EPA considers daily exposures up to 50 µg/kg to be safe, animal studies have demonstrated effects at much lower doses. Consumer advocacy groups recommend that individuals seeking to reduce their BPA exposure avoid canned foods and polycarbonate plastic containers, particularly those marked with resin identification code 7, unless explicitly labeled as BPA-free. To minimize the risk of BPA leaching into food or beverages, the National Toxicology Panel advises against microwaving food in plastic containers, placing plastics in dishwashers, or using harsh detergents. Consumption of soda, school lunches, and meals prepared outside the home has been statistically associated with higher urinary BPA levels. BPA is also used in the epoxy resin coatings of water pipes, particularly in older buildings, where such coatings are applied to prevent the replacement of deteriorating hot and cold water pipes. Children may be more vulnerable to BPA exposure than adults. A recent study found higher urinary BPA concentrations in young children compared to adults under typical exposure conditions. This increased susceptibility is likely due to their reduced ability to metabolize and eliminate xenobiotics, as well as their relatively higher daily exposure to BPA when adjusted for body weight. Infants fed liquid formula, especially from polycarbonate bottles, can consume up to 13 µg/kg/day of BPA. BPA has been rarely detected in infant powder formula, with only 1 out of 14 samples testing positive. While breastfeeding is the optimal source of nutrition for infants, it is not always feasible. The U.S. Department of Health & Human Services (HHS) has stated that the benefits of a stable source of good nutrition from infant formula outweigh the potential risks of BPA exposure. A 2010 study conducted in Austria, Switzerland, and Germany identified polycarbonate baby bottles as the primary source of BPA exposure for infants, while canned food was the main source for adults and teenagers. In the United States, growing concerns over BPA exposure in infants have led manufacturers to cease using BPA in plastic baby bottles. However, infants may still be exposed if fed using older or second-hand bottles manufactured before BPA was phased out. Another overlooked source of exposure occurs when pregnant women are exposed to BPA, which can subsequently expose the fetus. Animal studies have shown that BPA can be detected in the placenta and amniotic fluid of pregnant mice. BPA has also been found in the blood of 9 out of 10 umbilical cords tested. After birth, maternal exposure to BPA can continue to affect the infant through breast milk. To reduce their child’s exposure to BPA, mothers should aim to limit their own exposure during pregnancy and breastfeeding. Dietary intake is the primary source of BPA exposure, but accidental ingestion can also occur. A study in Japan tested plastic baby books for potential BPA leaching into saliva when chewed by infants. Although these findings have not been replicated, they raise concerns about whether BPA exposure can occur through chewing on certain books or toys. There is no consensus among scientists regarding a physiologically-based pharmacokinetic (PBPK) model for BPA in humans. The effects of BPA on an organism depend on the concentration of free BPA and the duration of cellular exposure. In the liver, BPA undergoes glucuronidation, where it is conjugated with glucuronic acid to form BPA-glucuronide (BPAG), reducing the amount of free BPA. However, BPAG can be deconjugated by beta-glucuronidase, an enzyme found in high concentrations in the placenta and other tissues. Free BPA can also be inactivated through sulfation, a process that can be reversed by arylsulfatase C. A 2010 in vitro study suggested that placental P-glycoprotein may efflux BPA from the placenta. The best methods for studying BPA’s effects remain under debate, with scientists holding differing opinions. A 2010 review of over 80 biomonitoring studies concluded that the general population is internally exposed to significant levels of unconjugated BPA, typically in the ng/mL blood range. Additionally, a 2009 study found that certain drugs, such as naproxen, salicylic acid, carbamazepine, and mefenamic acid, can significantly inhibit BPA glucuronidation in vitro. A 2010 study on rat embryos suggested that genistein may enhance the developmental toxicity of BPA. Environmental studies have shown that BPA can impact growth, reproduction, and development in aquatic organisms, with fish being the most sensitive species. Endocrine-related effects have been observed in fish, aquatic invertebrates, amphibians, and reptiles at environmentally relevant exposure levels lower than those required for acute toxicity. Reported values for endocrine-related effects vary widely but often fall within the range of 1 µg/L to 1 mg/L. BPA can contaminate the environment directly or through the degradation of BPA-containing products, such as ocean-borne plastic waste. As an environmental contaminant, BPA interferes with nitrogen fixation in the roots of leguminous plants associated with the bacterial symbiont Sinorhizobium meliloti. Despite a soil half-life of only 1–10 days, BPA’s ubiquity makes it a significant pollutant. According to Environment Canada, initial assessment shows that at low levels, bisphenol A can harm fish and organisms over time. Studies also indicate that BPA is currently present in municipal wastewater.
